What the agent captures: Name, role/title, and whether they order, approve, or neither.
Why it matters: A need recorded against someone who cannot buy is not a pipeline. Roles are captured well in hospitality and multifamily and barely at all in the other four verticals.
Evidence from the shared file: Role or title named in 28.79% of hospitality and 22.65% of multifamily notes, but only 6.92% in healthcare, 6.61% in public sector and 3.71% in trades [EV-U-01].

What the agent captures: Spoke with target / spoke with alternate / no contact. If no contact: who was met, what was left, when to return.
Why it matters: Around one call in ten reaches nobody. Today these often produce an empty or throwaway note, so the visit is spent and nothing is learned.
Evidence from the shared file: No-contact language in 10.45% of public sector, 10.27% of hospitality and 9.36% of multifamily notes [EV-U-02].

What the agent captures: For each planned topic: discussed / not discussed / deferred, plus the customer response.
Why it matters: The business plans by topic and needs to report by topic. Without per-topic status, campaign effectiveness cannot be measured.
Evidence from the shared file: All 445,015 calls carry planned topics, across 1,967 distinct topic strings [EV-U-03].

What the agent captures: Order placed, quote created (value and number), quote pending approval, return/credit, or none.
Why it matters: The one field that connects a conversation to revenue.
Evidence from the shared file: Quote language in 18.41% of multifamily notes, the highest in the file; order language in 10.3% of hospitality notes, also the highest [EV-U-04].

What the agent captures: Credit hold, aging invoices, PO not approved, portal ineligibility, account transfer.
Why it matters: Blockers are frequently the real reason nothing happened. Recorded as "no need" they look like disinterest and get worked wrongly.
Evidence from the shared file: Credit or invoice language in 3.67% of multifamily notes and PO or approval language in 3.96% - both the highest in the file [EV-U-05].

What the agent captures: Who they buy from instead and why: price, delivery speed, ease of ordering, existing contract.
Why it matters: The reason determines the response. Price pressure is not spread evenly - trades is roughly twice as price-driven as multifamily.
Evidence from the shared file: Price language in 18.35% of trades notes against 9.46% in multifamily; a competitor is named in 4.68% of multifamily notes, the highest rate in the file [EV-U-06].

What the agent captures: Backorder, mispick, damage, missing item, ETA request, warranty.
Why it matters: Service recovery is live on roughly one call in fifteen and is the fastest route to losing an account.
Evidence from the shared file: Service-failure language in 7.22% of multifamily and 6.58% of hospitality notes [EV-U-07].

What the agent captures: New manager, new ownership, new management company, contact departed.
Why it matters: Keeps the CRM current. A departed contact silently invalidates every future plan built on them.
Evidence from the shared file: Change language in 2.59% of hospitality and 2.33% of multifamily notes [EV-U-08].

What the agent captures: Only if explicitly stated. Never inferred from "soon" or "next visit".
Why it matters: The field that makes a note actionable. Most important in public sector, where approval cycles are longest.
Evidence from the shared file: Follow-up language in 14.46% of public sector notes, four points above any other vertical [EV-U-09].

What the agent captures: The vertical's countable unit: turns, keys, beds, sites, jobs, reorder cycles.
Why it matters: Turns a vague need into a forecastable quantity. Reps know these numbers and almost never write them down. This is the largest single gap the agent can close, and it is consistent across every vertical.
Evidence from the shared file: A quantified count appears in 2.17% of healthcare notes at best and 1.05% at worst - between one and two percent everywhere [EV-U-10].

What the agent captures: Where a repeat-purchase item is stocked, the on-hand or par quantity, and who notices when it runs out.
Why it matters: Converts a one-off order into a replenishment cadence. A project buys once; a stocked location reorders indefinitely.
Evidence from the shared file: Stocking language in 6.27% of trades notes, the highest in the file, against 2.74% in multifamily; explicit par language never exceeds 0.6% in any vertical [EV-U-11].
